title: Ride Concepts Livewire Shoe Review – Sam Hodges
content:
After blowing through pairs of MTB flat shoes every six months, Sam Hodges decided to give the Ride Concepts Livewire a try. Do the Livewire shoes hold up to daily thrashing on Moab’s techie trails? Read Sam’s review below…

Ride Concepts Livewire Quick Hits

  • $122
  • Colors: Charcoal (reviewed), Black, Olive
  • Sizes:
    • Men’s: 7-15
    • Women’s: 5-10
  • High Grip rubber outsole
  • Cup outsole is glued and stitched for durability and delivers ultimate pedal feel
  • Dual-density EVA insole provides additional support and cushioning
  • Traditional lace closure
  • Anti-bacterial mesh lining controls odor
  • TPU toe and heel protection with reinforced anti-abrasion film
  • Fully gusseted tongue
  • Outsole medial arch provides additional support for impact damping and power transfer
  • 400g per shoe (size M9)

About ten years ago, I started transitioning from climbing as my main form of recreation to biking; five years before that, I had transitioned from skateboarding to climbing. Backpacking has been a consistent form of getting outside between all of these activities. I still dabble in skating, climbing, and now backpack for a living. I’ve also added several new forms of recreation: packrafting, trail running, canyoneering, search and rescue, along with road biking, gravel biking, mountain biking, and bikepacking. It’s sick that for each of these activities, there is a specific shoe you need (or want) to do each of them comfortably or more efficiently. The downside is that shoes are expensive and don’t seem to be getting cheaper any time soon.

Like most people, after getting over the initial hurdle of buying a bike and all the other gear to start riding, I thought, “Surely one of the pairs of shoes I already own MUST be able to do double duty biking.” I shredded multiple pairs of skate and running shoes before moving on to approach shoes, which lasted a little longer (but not by much). A couple years into riding as my primary activity, I finally gave in and purchased some mountain bike-specific shoes, adding yet another pair of shoes to the ever-growing arsenal. Since then I’ve largely stuck with 5.10 Freerider Pros, after being disappointed by the longevity and grip I found with other options on the market in my earlier days of riding. The aggressive and technical style in Moab and my preference for flats means that I’m going through about two pairs a year. After about a decade of riding almost daily, I figured it might be time to branch out. In the last five years, the market for shoes has expanded with a wider range of rubber compounds and more intentional styles being developed. After hearing good things from friends and being drawn in by the slimmed-down and low-profile aesthetics, I decided to test out the Ride Concepts Livewire flat pedal shoes.

The Livewire is a slim skate-style shoe (which isn’t easy to accomplish with molded heel and toe protection) and doesn’t fall into either the heavily padded downhill or more athletic hiker style categories. The soles feature a Ride Concepts High Grip rubber compound, which I found to be slightly stiffer and more durable than other options I’ve ridden. The sole of the Livewire has a slightly raised honeycomb pattern, which allows for pedal pins to grip easily and the shoes to find their place without feeling forced or needing to constantly readjust for better grip. That said, they also don’t feel so locked in that readjustments are difficult. While I enjoyed the feel on the bike, hiking in them is a different experience. I found myself slipping around and unable to get good footing when hiking on packed trails or on sandstone slick rock. The fully gusseted tongue prevents rocks and dirt from getting into the shoe when hiking or biking, which is a huge plus. It’s pretty annoying having to stop to empty out your shoes when biking. Due to the gusseted tongue, they can feel a little warm and constricting. This wasn’t a dealbreaker for me, since I like my shoes to feel tight around my feet, but that might not be everyone’s preference.

I’ve put these shoes through their paces over the last 7 months and have been pleased overall. Riding in Moab, I spend the majority of my time on singletrack out of the saddle, climbing or descending technical rocky trails. Between the terrain, distance, and riding style, the sole of these shoes lasted longer than expected. The RC Livewire has blown past my typical 6-month timeline and still has a good amount of life in them. The price point of the RC Livewire is another huge benefit, as I’m used to spending $40.00 more per pair. One of the best things you can say about a shoe is that I never found myself thinking about them. They fit true to size, feel secure around my feet and on the pedals, and I haven’t felt my feet fatiguing during longer, more demanding rides. The grip and stiffness of the sole exceeded what I have come to expect from a modern MTB-specific shoe. Overall, I am impressed with the durability and price point. If you find yourself needing to add yet another pair of shoes to your collection that won’t break the bank, these will look good, and you might be pleasantly surprised by how long they last.

Pros

  • Cheaper than most flat pedal shoes at $122.00
  • Durable soles that provide exceptional grip
  • Low-profile design and neutral colorways that look good on the trail.
  • True to size, with sizes ranging from 7-15, including half sizes.

Cons

  • Not the best in grip for longer hike-a-bike adventures.
  • Can feel a little warm because of the fully gusseted tongue.
  • Narrow fit.
